chunks: OIS vs EIS image stabilization. The question: What is optical image stabilization (OIS)? What is electronic image stabilization? What is the difference (EIS)?
What are each of their applications?
When your hand shakes, the camera rotates a little, and the picture smears.
Optical image stabilization, OIS, uses a gyroscope to sense the shake and physically moves the lens or sensor the opposite way while the shutter is open.
Electronic image stabilization, EIS, works in software: it crops each frame and slides the crop window to cancel the motion. OIS keeps each frame sharp.
EIS only smooths the video afterward.
Carry a cup of coffee on a bumpy bus. You can move your hand against each bump to keep the cup level, which is OIS.
Or you can let the cup shake, then slide a small frame over a larger photo of it, so the picture looks steady, which is EIS.
The frame fix cannot unsmear a blur, because the blur is already in each photo. It also needs spare margin at the edges, so the result is cropped.
Blur grows linearly with exposure. At the defaults, without stabilization you stay under 1 pixel only up to about 5 milliseconds (1/200 seconds).
With 20 decibels of OIS suppression the limit moves to about 51 milliseconds (1/20 seconds), a factor of 10, which is log 2 10 equals 3. 3 stops.
Drag the OIS suppression to 30 decibels: the stabilized 1-pixel limit moves to about 0. 16 seconds, five stops beyond the unstabilized 5 milliseconds.
Raise the shake rate to 8°/s and the unstabilized limit collapses to about 1. 3 milliseconds.
Gyroscope: a sensor that measures how fast the camera is rotating. Motion blur: smearing caused by the image moving across the sensor during the exposure.
Focal length: the distance from the lens to the sensor when focused far away. A longer one magnifies shake more. Stop: one doubling of exposure time.
A phone camera has a 5. 6 mm focal length. The hand rotates at 2 degrees per second during a 1/15 seconds exposure.
The camera turns by 2/15 of a degree, and the image on the sensor smears by about 13 µm, roughly 13 pixels of 1 µm. Say OIS cancels 90 percent of that shake.
The same blur now allows an exposure 10 times longer, about 3. 3 stops. EIS could not do this, because it only shifts finished frames. That is the whole idea.
"OIS physically moves the lens or sensor, driven by a gyro in a closed loop with position feedback, so the image stays still on the sensor during the exposure.
That removes blur in each frame, which helps photos and low light.
EIS is software: it uses gyro and image data to shift and crop frames after capture, so it has no moving parts, but it can't fix blur within an exposure and it costs field of view.
OIS is mostly for stills, EIS for video, and high-end phones use both together."
